record.original_question: What progenitor systems actually produce the main classes of gamma-ray bursts? More specifically, which stellar or compact-object channels generate massive-star GRBs and compact-star GRBs, given that current evidence is indirect, only a small and biased subset of long GRBs have secure supernova associations, and some short-duration or high-redshift events do not fit a simple neutron-star-merger picture?

evidence.quote: The progenitors of GRBs are not identified, and it will be very difficult to identify them.
Despite the indirect supports to the merger scenarios mentioned above, following observational facts raise cautions to take the merger progenitors as truth.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are intense, transient flashes of cosmic gamma radiation, conventionally divided by their prompt-emission duration into two main classes: long-duration GRBs (T90 ≳ 2 s), often called massive-star or Type II GRBs, and short-duration GRBs (T90 ≲ 2 s), often called compact-star or Type I GRBs. The prevailing hypothesis associates long GRBs with the gravitational collapse of rapidly rotating, massive stars (the "collapsar" channel, which can produce Type Ic broad-line supernovae), and short GRBs with the coalescence of compact-object binaries (double neutron stars or neutron-star–black-hole systems).

However, only a small, observationally biased subset of long GRBs have secure supernova associations, several short-duration and high-redshift bursts do not fit a simple neutron-star-merger picture, and some long-duration events show kilonova-like signatures expected from compact mergers rather than hypernova signatures.

Problem. Identify, from first principles and observational diagnostics, the actual progenitor systems that produce each main class of GRB. Concretely:

(a) Determine the full set of stellar or compact-object channels that give rise to massive-star (long-duration) GRBs, including conditions on stellar mass, metallicity, rotation, and binarity required to launch a successful relativistic jet, and explain the apparent paucity of secure supernova associations.

(b) Determine the full set of compact-object channels (e.g., NS–NS, NS–BH, WD–NS, WD–BH, accretion-induced collapse) that give rise to compact-star (short-duration or merger-driven) GRBs, and account for short or high-redshift events that are inconsistent with a standard neutron-star-merger origin.

(c) Provide observational discriminants — using prompt light curves, afterglow spectra, host-galaxy properties, offsets, and multi-messenger (gravitational-wave, kilonova) signatures — that uniquely map an individual burst to its progenitor channel, replacing duration-based classification with progenitor-based classification.
artifact.status_search_result: The progenitor question has been partially resolved since the original posing. The 2017 multi-messenger event GW170817/GRB 170817A confirmed binary neutron-star mergers as one channel for short GRBs, and several long GRBs have secure broad-line Type Ic supernova associations supporting the collapsar channel. However, anomalous events such as GRB 211211A and GRB 191019A (long-duration bursts with kilonova-like signatures suggesting merger origins) and GRB 200826A (a short burst with a supernova association) demonstrate that a complete, progenitor-based classification mapping all GRBs to specific stellar/compact-object channels remains open as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Gamma-Ray Burst Progenitors (Space Science Reviews)
status_evidence.snippet: Bimodal duration distribution leads to two distinct progenitors: compact star mergers for short GRBs and collapsars for long GRBs.
status_evidence.claim: The standard two-channel picture is broadly supported but with notable exceptions.

status_evidence.title: A nearby long gamma-ray burst from a merger of compact objects (Nature, 2022)
status_evidence.snippet: GRB 211211A: a 51-second long GRB whose afterglow shows kilonova features indicative of a compact-object merger.
status_evidence.claim: Some long-duration GRBs arise from compact-object mergers, complicating duration-based classification.

status_evidence.title: Progenitors of Low-redshift Gamma-Ray Bursts (ApJL, 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: Recent study revisiting the progenitor channels of low-redshift GRBs.
status_evidence.claim: Active research continues into mapping individual GRBs to progenitor channels.
